title: The Reciter (Tanna) of the School of Rabbi So-and-so, or “A Reciter Taught before Rabbi So-and-so”
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: Model-assisted translation, editorially reviewed; publication authorized by Joshua Waxman.

paragraphs: Hyman has already explained in several places that every head of an academy had a reciter (tanna) or reciters (tannaim) (even at the end of the period of the Amoraim) who sat before him and were very expert in the baraitot by heart. When a baraita was needed (for the most part they studied orally), he was like a living book and would tell his teacher the wording of the baraita. But since their whole concern was only to have the wording of the baraita fluent in their mouths, they sometimes erred in a word; and this is why we find many times in the Talmud that the head of the academy said to him, “Do not teach it so,” or “Delete it.” Hyman applies to them the statement in [Sotah 22a](https://www.sefaria.org/Sotah.22a.7): “The Tannaim destroy the world, for they rule halakhah from their mishnah” — this does not refer to our masters, the sages of the Mishnah or the baraitot, but to these reciters.
So [Rashi on Chullin 15a](https://www.sefaria.org/Rashi_on_Chullin.15a.13.2), s.v. Atu; see also [Rashi on Bava Metzia 34a](https://www.sefaria.org/Rashi_on_Bava_Metzia.34a.17.2), s.v. LeTannai.

So it is cited in the [Epistle of Rav Sherira Gaon](https://www.sefaria.org/Epistle_of_Rav_Sherira_Gaon.1.42), where he says: “And the Tannaim too learned them among themselves, such as Achi, the Tanna of the school of Rabbi Chiyya, and Bar Ashyan, the Tanna of the school of Rabbi Ami.”[^1]

notes.text: [Rashi on Sotah 22a](https://www.sefaria.org/Rashi_on_Sotah.22a.7.2) explains that rulings based on memorized texts can be mistaken when the reciter lacks the reasons or does not know which view governs. The Chullin gloss describes an audience for Rav’s teaching. The Bava Metzia gloss discusses reciters of the collections of Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Oshaya. The consulted Epistle gives Achi and Ashyan as examples. Hyman quotes the second as Bar Ashyan and draws on these passages for his broader account of the professional reciter.
